notes.front: In the Nexus Guide, what are the levels of decomposition that Product Backlog items pass through?
notes.back: Steps from very large and vague requests down to actionable work that a single Scrum Team could deliver inside a Sprint.
notes.explanation: The Nexus Guide describes this during Cross-Team Refinement, where the Product Backlog is decomposed so that dependencies become transparent.
notes.evidence: The Product Backlog must be decomposed so that dependencies are transparent, identified across teams, and removed or minimized. Product Backlog items pass through different levels of decomposition from very large and vague requests to actionable work that a single Scrum Team could deliver inside a Sprint.
notes.example: Like a holiday plan that starts as “tour Scotland” and is broken down until one line reads “Tuesday: morning train to Inverness”.

notes.front: In the Scrum Guide's short description of Scrum, a Product Owner orders the work for a {{c1::complex problem}} into a Product Backlog.
notes.explanation: Scrum is described as a framework for adaptive solutions to complex problems, and ordering the Product Backlog is the Product Owner's first step in its loop.
notes.evidence: Scrum is a lightweight framework that helps people, teams and organizations generate value through adaptive solutions for complex problems. In a nutshell, Scrum requires a Scrum Master to foster an environment where: - A Product Owner orders the work for a complex problem into a Product Backlog.

notes.front: Management hands a new Product Owner a fixed list of 200 requirements, ordered by which department asked first, and says, “Just track progress against it.” What does the Scrum Guide say about this list?
notes.back: C: The Product Backlog is an emergent, ordered list, and the Product Owner orders it
notes.choices:
A) It is fine: the Product Backlog is fixed once management approves it
B) The order should stay first-come, first-served to be fair
C) The Product Backlog is an emergent, ordered list, and the Product Owner orders it
D) The Developers should reorder it at each Daily Scrum
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide calls the Product Backlog emergent. B: ordering Product Backlog items is part of the Product Owner's accountability. D: the Daily Scrum inspects progress toward the Sprint Goal; ordering is the Product Owner's.
notes.explanation: The Guide describes the Product Backlog as emergent and ordered, and as the single source of the Scrum Team's work.
notes.evidence: The Product Backlog is an emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product. It is the single source of work undertaken by the Scrum Team.

notes.front: Which is the Product Backlog's commitment in Scrum: “ready for selection” or the Product Goal?
notes.back: The Product Goal; “ready for selection” describes items that can be Done within one Sprint.
notes.explanation: The Guide names one commitment per artifact, and readiness is not among them.
notes.evidence: For the Product Backlog it is the Product Goal. - For the Sprint Backlog it is the Sprint Goal. - For the Increment it is the Definition of Done.

notes.front: Two days before Sprint Planning, the top Product Backlog item is still a one-line wish that nobody could get Done in a Sprint. What is the usual way to get it ready for selection?
notes.back: D: Refine it: break it down and add detail until it can be Done within one Sprint
notes.choices:
A) Select it anyway and work out the details during the Sprint
B) Add a formal “Definition of Ready” as a fourth Scrum commitment
C) Have the Product Owner write a full specification alone and assign it
D) Refine it: break it down and add detail until it can be Done within one Sprint
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Guide names three commitments; readiness is not one of them. C: the Developers select items; the Product Owner does not assign them. A: items that can be Done within one Sprint are the ones deemed ready for selection.
notes.explanation: The Guide says items usually acquire the transparency to be ready for selection after refining activities.
notes.evidence: Product Backlog items that can be Done by the Scrum Team within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in a Sprint Planning event. They usually acquire this degree of transparency after refining activities.

notes.front: According to the Scrum Guide, what does refining selected items during Sprint Planning increase?
notes.back: Understanding and confidence.
notes.explanation: The Guide says the Scrum Team may refine items while the Developers select them for the Sprint.
notes.evidence: Through discussion with the Product Owner, the Developers select items from the Product Backlog to include in the current Sprint. The Scrum Team may refine these items during this process, which increases understanding and confidence.

notes.front: At Sprint Planning the Developers find the second item unclear. The Product Owner says, “Refinement is not allowed here; it has to wait for next Sprint.” What does the Scrum Guide say?
notes.back: B: The Scrum Team may refine items during Sprint Planning, which increases understanding and confidence
notes.choices:
A) The Product Owner is right: refinement only happens between events
B) The Scrum Team may refine items during Sprint Planning, which increases understanding and confidence
C) Only the Scrum Master may refine items during Sprint Planning
D) The Developers must take the item unrefined
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide explicitly allows refining items during this part of Sprint Planning. C: the Guide gives this to the Scrum Team. D: refining while selecting is what raises the team's understanding and confidence.
notes.explanation: The Guide places refinement inside the selection of items, so unclear items can be clarified there.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Team may refine these items during this process, which increases understanding and confidence.

notes.front: At Sprint Planning, how do the Product Owner's and the Developers' parts differ in choosing the Sprint's items?
notes.back: The Developers select the items; they do so through discussion with the Product Owner.
notes.explanation: Selection belongs to the people who will do the work, while the Product Owner takes part in the discussion.
notes.evidence: Through discussion with the Product Owner, the Developers select items from the Product Backlog to include in the current Sprint.

notes.front: A Product Owner arrives at Sprint Planning with the Sprint's items already chosen and each one assigned to a named Developer. What is wrong?
notes.back: C: The Developers select the items, through discussion with the Product Owner, and decide who does what
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: assigning work is part of ordering the Product Backlog
B) Only the assignment; choosing the items is the Product Owner's call
C) The Developers select the items, through discussion with the Product Owner, and decide who does what
D) The Scrum Master should have assigned them instead
notes.choicesExplained: A: ordering sets the order of the Product Backlog; selection and who does what are the Developers'. B: the Guide says the Developers select the items. D: Scrum Teams are self-managing: they decide internally who does what.
notes.explanation: The Guide gives selection to the Developers, with the Product Owner taking part through discussion.
notes.evidence: Through discussion with the Product Owner, the Developers select items from the Product Backlog to include in the current Sprint.

notes.front: Based on their past performance and capacity, the Developers forecast six items. The Product Owner pushes for nine “to show ambition”. What does the Scrum Guide say?
notes.back: D: The Developers select how much to take on, through discussion with the Product Owner
notes.choices:
A) The Product Owner decides how much, as owner of the Product Backlog
B) The Scrum Master should split the difference at seven or eight
C) The team must take nine and lower the Definition of Done to fit
D) The Developers select how much to take on, through discussion with the Product Owner
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide gives selection to the Developers. B: the Scrum Master does not decide the Sprint's selection. C: the Developers are required to conform to the Definition of Done.
notes.explanation: The Guide says knowing their past performance, capacity and Definition of Done makes the Developers more confident in their Sprint forecasts.
notes.evidence: However, the more the Developers know about their past performance, their upcoming capacity, and their Definition of Done, the more confident they will be in their Sprint forecasts.

notes.front: The top Product Backlog item reads “Rebuild the customer portal”, which would take months. The next Sprint Planning is soon. What should the Product Owner and Developers do with it?
notes.back: C: Decompose it until the top pieces are actionable work one Scrum Team could deliver inside a Sprint
notes.choices:
A) Select it as it is and extend the Sprint until it is finished
B) Move it to the bottom, since large items cannot be in a Product Backlog
C) Decompose it until the top pieces are actionable work one Scrum Team could deliver inside a Sprint
D) Hand it to a separate project team outside Scrum
notes.choicesExplained: A: Sprints are fixed length; the item must be broken down instead. B: large, vague requests are an early level of decomposition, not forbidden. D: the Product Backlog is the single source of work for the Scrum Team.
notes.explanation: The Nexus Guide describes items passing from very large and vague requests to work a single Scrum Team could deliver inside a Sprint.
notes.evidence: Product Backlog items pass through different levels of decomposition from very large and vague requests to actionable work that a single Scrum Team could deliver inside a Sprint.

notes.front: A stakeholder insists that every one of the 300 Product Backlog items be written in full detail now, “so the plan is complete”. How should the Product Owner answer?
notes.back: A: Items move from large and vague to actionable as they are decomposed; refinement is ongoing, not done once
notes.choices:
A) Items move from large and vague to actionable as they are decomposed; refinement is ongoing, not done once
B) Refuse any refinement until items reach the top
C) Let the stakeholder write the details directly into the Product Backlog
D) Agree, and detail all 300 items before the next Sprint
notes.choicesExplained: D: the Guide calls refinement an ongoing activity; items are decomposed over time. B: refinement is ongoing and adds detail such as description, order and size as needed. C: those wanting to change the Product Backlog do so by trying to convince the Product Owner.
notes.explanation: The Nexus Guide describes decomposition in levels, from vague requests to actionable work, so detail grows as items are broken down.
notes.evidence: Product Backlog items pass through different levels of decomposition from very large and vague requests to actionable work that a single Scrum Team could deliver inside a Sprint.

notes.front: Two items have similar value, but the reporting item cannot work until the data-export item exists. How should the Product Owner handle this?
notes.back: B: Make the dependency transparent and order so the export comes first, or work with the Developers to remove the dependency
notes.choices:
A) Ignore the dependency; order strictly by value
B) Make the dependency transparent and order so the export comes first, or work with the Developers to remove the dependency
C) Order the reporting item first to create pressure
D) Let each Developer pick whichever item they prefer
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Nexus Guide asks for dependencies to be made transparent and removed or minimised. C: that orders work that cannot yet deliver value. D: ordering the Product Backlog is the Product Owner's accountability.
notes.explanation: The Nexus Guide says the Product Backlog must be decomposed so that dependencies are transparent, identified and removed or minimised.
notes.evidence: The Product Backlog must be decomposed so that dependencies are transparent, identified across teams, and removed or minimized.

notes.front: The Product Goal is to let tenants report repairs online. A stakeholder offers a high-value idea for a rent-comparison tool, unrelated to the goal. A moderate item finishes photo upload for repair reports. How should the Product Owner order them?
notes.back: D: Photo upload first, since the Product Backlog should define what fulfils the Product Goal, unless the Product Owner decides to change the goal
notes.choices:
A) Let the stakeholder decide, since the idea is theirs
B) Rent comparison first, because its value is higher
C) Work on both in parallel as two Product Goals
D) Photo upload first, since the Product Backlog should define what fulfils the Product Goal, unless the Product Owner decides to change the goal
notes.choicesExplained: B: the rest of the Product Backlog emerges to define what will fulfil the current Product Goal. C: the Scrum Team fulfils or abandons one objective before taking on the next. A: ordering is the Product Owner's decision.
notes.explanation: The Guide ties the content of the Product Backlog to the Product Goal it is meant to fulfil.
notes.evidence: The Product Goal is in the Product Backlog. The rest of the Product Backlog emerges to define “what” will fulfill the Product Goal.

notes.front: A manager proposes ordering the Product Backlog strictly by the date each request arrived, “so nobody can complain”. What should guide the Product Owner's ordering instead?
notes.back: A: Maximising the value of the product, which the Product Owner is accountable for
notes.choices:
A) Maximising the value of the product, which the Product Owner is accountable for
B) The date of each request, as proposed
C) Whoever shouts loudest, since that shows urgency
D) The Developers' preferences, since they do the work
notes.choicesExplained: B: arrival order says nothing about value; the Product Owner is accountable for maximising value. C: the Product Owner represents the needs of many stakeholders, not only the loudest. D: the Developers select items for a Sprint; ordering is the Product Owner's accountability.
notes.explanation: The Guide makes the Product Owner accountable for maximising the value of the product, so value, not arrival date, is the test.
notes.evidence: The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team.

notes.front: A large, uncertain feature would take four Sprints. A two-day test could show whether customers want it at all. Where should the Product Owner order the test?
notes.back: A: Early, before the large feature, to validate the critical assumption cheaply
notes.choices:
A) Early, before the large feature, to validate the critical assumption cheaply
B) Nowhere: the feature is obviously valuable
C) In a separate research backlog outside Scrum
D) After the feature, to confirm it worked
notes.choicesExplained: D: testing afterwards spends the whole cost before learning whether the feature has value. B: the EBM Guide says every feature really represents a hypothesis about value. C: the Product Backlog is the single source of work for the Scrum Team.
notes.explanation: The EBM Guide says the whole feature need not be built to judge its value; building enough to validate critical assumptions may be sufficient.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Hypotheses, Experiments, Features, and Requirements”, p. 7
notes.evidence: The entire feature or requirement need not actually be built to determine whether it is valuable; it may be sufficient for a team to simply build enough of it to validate critical assumptions that would prove or disprove its value.

notes.front: A Product Owner wants a Product Backlog item for a “save for later” button to make its assumption about value explicit. Which wording does that best?
notes.back: B: We believe adding “save for later” will lead to more returning shoppers completing purchases
notes.choices:
A) Add a “save for later” button, estimated at five days
B) We believe adding “save for later” will lead to more returning shoppers completing purchases
C) Add a “save for later” button because the chief executive wants it
D) Add a “save for later” button that matches the competitor's design
notes.choicesExplained: A: this states the work and its size, not the expected outcome. C: a sponsor's wish is a belief, not an explicit hypothesis about an outcome. D: copying a design does not state what outcome is expected.
notes.explanation: The EBM Guide describes a hypothesis as a belief that doing something will lead to something else.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Hypotheses, Experiments, Features, and Requirements”, p. 7
notes.evidence: A hypothesis is a belief that doing something will lead to something else, such as delivering feature X will lead to outcome Y.

notes.front: An experiment shows the new onboarding screens did not change how many users finish sign-up. Three more onboarding items sit near the top of the Product Backlog. What should the Product Owner do?
notes.back: B: Adapt: reconsider or reorder the remaining items, and use what was learned to design new experiments
notes.choices:
A) Build the remaining items anyway, as planned
B) Adapt: reconsider or reorder the remaining items, and use what was learned to design new experiments
C) Stop running experiments, since they can fail
D) Hide the result so stakeholders do not lose faith
notes.choicesExplained: A: the result is evidence against the hypothesis; ignoring it wastes the learning. D: the EBM Guide says a failed experiment is not a bad thing. C: the Guide says what you learn helps you devise experiments that may yield better results.
notes.explanation: The EBM Guide says failing to reach a goal because an experiment did not produce the expected results is not a bad thing, and the learning feeds new experiments.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Inspecting and Adapting Based on Experiment Results”, p. 12
notes.evidence: sometimes you’ll fail to reach your Immediate Tactical Goal because your experiment did not produce the results you had expected. This is not a bad thing, and what you learned helps you to devise new experiments that may yield better results.

notes.front: A stakeholder says a feature needs no testing because “all the executives believe customers will love it”. What does the EBM Guide say about that belief?
notes.back: A: It is an assumption until customers validate it
notes.choices:
A) It is an assumption until customers validate it
B) Executive belief is enough validation
C) It becomes valid once the feature is in the Product Backlog
D) It can be validated by the Developers' estimate
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Guide says beliefs in what is valuable are merely assumptions until customers validate them. C: putting it in the backlog does not validate it. D: an estimate measures effort, not whether customers find value.
notes.explanation: The EBM Guide warns that organisations can spend a lot on features only to find customers do not share their view of the value.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Hypotheses, Experiments, Features, and Requirements”, p. 7
notes.evidence: Organizations can spend a lot of money implementing features (distinguishing characteristics) and other requirements in products,4 only to find that customers don’t share the company’s opinion on their value; beliefs in what is valuable are merely assumptions until they are validated by customers.

notes.front: The Developers ask for time to clean up “quick and dirty” code that now slows every change. Stakeholders want only new features. How should the Product Owner weigh the clean-up?
notes.back: D: As real Product Backlog work: technical debt hurts the delivery of value and adds avoidable waste and risk
notes.choices:
A) Postpone it until the product is retired
B) Ignore it, because only features create value
C) Let the Developers do it secretly inside other items
D) As real Product Backlog work: technical debt hurts the delivery of value and adds avoidable waste and risk
notes.choicesExplained: B: the EBM Guide says technical debt has an undesirable impact on the delivery of value. C: hiding work undermines a Product Backlog that is transparent, visible and understood. A: the debt keeps adding waste and risk while it stays.
notes.explanation: The EBM Guide describes technical debt as an undesirable impact on the delivery of value and an avoidable increase in waste and risk.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Appendix: Example Key Value Measures”, p. 16
notes.evidence: It creates an undesirable impact on the delivery of value and an avoidable increase in waste and risk.

notes.front: The team is interrupted almost daily to fix problems in the installed product, and fewer new capabilities ship each Sprint. Which Key Value Area is suffering most directly, per the EBM Guide?
notes.back: B: Ability to Innovate
notes.choices:
A) Current Value
B) Ability to Innovate
C) Unrealized Value
D) Time-to-Market
notes.choicesExplained: A: Current Value looks at the value customers experience today, not at capacity to deliver new capabilities. C: Unrealized Value measures potential future value, not what is blocking delivery. D: Time-to-Market measures how quickly the organisation can deliver and learn from feedback; the Guide files time spent remedying poor quality, and interruptions to fix an installed product, under Ability to Innovate.
notes.explanation: The Guide names time spent remedying poor product quality among the things that impede an organisation from delivering new capabilities.
notes.source: The Evidence-Based Management Guide (May 2024), “Ability to Innovate (A2I)”, p. 10
notes.evidence: A variety of things can impede an organization from being able to deliver new capabilities and value: spending too much time remedying poor product quality,

notes.front: Mid-Sprint, the Developers find one selected item is twice as big as expected. They can still meet the Sprint Goal if a lower-value item is dropped. What should happen?
notes.back: D: The Developers collaborate with the Product Owner to renegotiate the Sprint Backlog's scope without affecting the Sprint Goal
notes.choices:
A) The Developers drop the item on their own
B) The team extends the Sprint by a week
C) The Product Owner cancels the Sprint
D) The Developers collaborate with the Product Owner to renegotiate the Sprint Backlog's scope without affecting the Sprint Goal
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide has them collaborate with the Product Owner on scope. C: cancellation is for a Sprint Goal that becomes obsolete, which this one is not. B: Sprints are fixed length events.
notes.explanation: The Guide says that when work turns out different than expected, the Developers collaborate with the Product Owner on scope, and the Sprint Goal stays.
notes.evidence: If the work turns out to be different than they expected, they collaborate with the Product Owner to negotiate the scope of the Sprint Backlog within the Sprint without affecting the Sprint Goal.

notes.front: Mid-Sprint, the Product Owner wants to add an item unrelated to the Sprint Goal. The Developers say it would push out work the Sprint Goal needs. What should the Product Owner do?
notes.back: B: Order it in the Product Backlog for a later Sprint, since no changes may endanger the Sprint Goal
notes.choices:
A) Insist it goes in now, as the Product Owner has authority over scope
B) Order it in the Product Backlog for a later Sprint, since no changes may endanger the Sprint Goal
C) Ask the Developers to work overtime and keep both
D) Replace the Sprint Goal with the new item
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide says no changes are made that would endanger the Sprint Goal. D: the Sprint Goal is set at Sprint Planning; it is not swapped for one item mid-Sprint. C: the Guide's rule protects the Sprint Goal; overtime does not make the change safe.
notes.explanation: The Guide's rule for the Sprint is that no changes are made that would endanger the Sprint Goal.
notes.evidence: During the Sprint: - No changes are made that would endanger the Sprint Goal;

notes.front: Halfway through the Sprint, the Product Owner learns from a user interview that a selected item can be simpler than written. May the Product Owner and Developers change its scope now?
notes.back: D: Yes: scope may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner as more is learned
notes.choices:
A) No: selected items are frozen until the Sprint ends
B) Only at the Sprint Review
C) Only if the Scrum Master approves
D) Yes: scope may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner as more is learned
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide says scope may be clarified and renegotiated during the Sprint. C: the Guide places this with the Product Owner, not the Scrum Master. B: the Guide allows clarification during the Sprint as more is learned.
notes.explanation: The Guide's Sprint rules expect scope to be clarified as learning happens, with the Product Owner involved.
notes.evidence: Scope may be clarified and renegotiated with the Product Owner as more is learned.

notes.front: The Developers will meet the Sprint Goal three days early and have spare capacity. What does the Scrum Guide allow?
notes.back: D: Update the Sprint Backlog as more is learned, working with the Product Owner on any extra scope
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: the Sprint Backlog cannot change after Sprint Planning
B) End the Sprint early and start the next one
C) The Product Owner assigns extra items to named Developers
D) Update the Sprint Backlog as more is learned, working with the Product Owner on any extra scope
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide says the Sprint Backlog is updated throughout the Sprint. B: Sprints are fixed length events. C: the Developers decide how to do their work; the Product Owner does not assign tasks.
notes.explanation: The Guide calls the Sprint Backlog a real-time picture that is updated throughout the Sprint as more is learned.
notes.evidence: It is a highly visible, real-time picture of the work that the Developers plan to accomplish during the Sprint in order to achieve the Sprint Goal. Consequently, the Sprint Backlog is updated throughout the Sprint as more is learned.
